qtr.text: 2.1.2. Stress is usually placed at the end of the word form — nominal (the exceptions make up a small list) and verbal. Most morphological postpositive markers are stressed. Unstressed are the markers: nominal — the prepositive object marker š(ə)-/ž(ə)- and the postpositive attributive -i; verbal — the detachable person markers, the evidential particle -ta/-da/-a. Also unstressed are the derivational suffixes -aϑ, -yo and the emphatic marker -i/-e. [...] The phonetic realisation of stress has not been investigated. Word stress is weak, subordinate to phrasal stress.

146.tone: Four contrastive surface tones (High, Falling, Mid, Low). Initial syllables bear High or Falling; Falling never occurs non-initially and High occurs non-initially only when preceded by a High, so non-initial syllables are otherwise Mid or Low (Bell 1993:26). Bell argues from duration, vowel quality and pitch that initial stress is independent of the tones (p.32).

morph.stmt: Sutton 2014:299,304: the languages are 'polysynthetic... largely agglutinative... many of these bound grammatical morphemes being better deemed clitics than affixes', with the shared verb template 'PRON. PROCL. - ADV. - INC. NOUN - INC. VERB - MAIN VERB - VAL/TAM - SUB. ENCL.' and nouns that 'may take a number-marking suffix... an agent case marker may be attached, following the number marker, and all of the languages have postpositional enclitics' (p.301-302): i.e. Towa person/number indexation (and negation, inverse l-) is procliticised/prefixed before the stem, while number, case, voice, TAM and subordination are suffixal/enclitic or fused at the right edge of the stem.

tn.quote: There are four contrastive surface tones: High, Falling, Mid, and Low. Initial syllables have either High or Falling tone. The Falling tone never occurs in subsequent syllables, and the High tone only occurs in a noninitial syllable if it is preceded by a High tone. Thus noninitial syllables have either a Mid or Low tone, except in the case where there is a sequence of High tones from the beginning of the word. ... (The tonebearing units are syllables, since long vowels do not behave differently with respect to tonal assignment than short vowels.)

Stress falls on the syllable preceding the last overtly filled coda within the stress domain: final syllable if closed (consonant-final), penult if the word ends in a vowel (Colarusso 1992:17; Matasović p.12). 150.dq: Stress is a mixture of strong percussion and a slight rise in pitch. 2.5.1. Nouns and Pronouns On nouns and pronouns it is confined to the last stem morpheme (10a, b, c, f), and does not shift back to most affixes (10d). ... In either (10) or (11) stress must always fall before a coda that is overtly filled; that is, final vowels cannot receive normal stress.
150.dloc: Colarusso 1992:16-17, sec. 2.5-2.5.2 (book pp. 16-17 of the UCalgary Press open-access ch. 2); Gordon 2002:544, Appendix 1, row "Final (of root) | Kabardian | North Caucasian"
150.heavy: Heavy (stress-bearing) domain-final syllable = one with an overtly filled coda (Colarusso 1992:17: 'stress must always fall before a coda that is overtly filled; that is, final vowels cannot receive normal stress') OR a surface word-final long [ɑˑ] (Colarusso 1992:36: naked past-tense passives ending in [ɑˑ] 'are stressed as though [ɑˑ] ended in a glide or consonant', which he derives from underlying /-aɣ/ -> /aɦ/, i.e. a glide coda; Matasović p.12: penult retraction only 'for words ending in a' (short a in his a/ā transcription), pret. -ā- is stress-bearing). Light = domain-final open syllable in short a (or ə). Vowel length elsewhere plays no stated role, and Matasović p.12 notes open-syllable length itself partly follows stress ('accented vowels in open syllables are lengthened (a becomes ā)'), so the CVV leg is surface-true but analysed by Colarusso as CVC underlyingly.
150.dflt: penult of the stress domain when the domain-final syllable is open with a short vowel
150.prule: Within the stress domain (last stem morpheme on nouns/pronouns; on verbs the stem plus purely verbal suffixes, excluding plural, gerundive/participial and predicative/complementiser endings and affirmative -s'), stress falls on the final syllable if it is closed by an overt coda or ends in a surface long [a:] (Colarusso: underlying glide coda), otherwise on the penult ('the syllable before the last root consonant'); grammatical suffixes are mostly unstressed, but some verbal suffixes (pret. -a:-, fut. -nwə-) carry stress.
150.srule: Colarusso 1992:16 (impressionistic, optional, non-rhythmic): 'Often a secondary stress can be heard either on the root or the syllable before the primary stress' (11b [yèpƛá·ś], 11c [se·pƛìža·ǧa·śerét]), and a few affixes, e.g. -ə̀y 'even' (10e /pśáaśa-ha-m-r-ə̀y/), carry a distinct secondary stress. Superseded by the instrumental study of Gordon & Applebaum 2010a (words of 2-5 syllables, 7 speakers): 'No evidence was found for secondary stresses' (pretonic vowels do not differ by distance from the stress); Gordon & Applebaum 2023: 'one prominent syllable and no rhythmic secondary stresses', the prominence of -əj 'even' left open (stress, intonation or lexical).

morph.stmt: Matasović 2010:7, 17, 35-36: Kabardian has 'an extremely simple vowel system, a complex prefixation system and the S(ubject) O(bject) V(erb) order'; it 'is a polysynthetic language... Nouns can take a relatively small number of different forms, but the verbal complex typically contains a large number of affixes'; 'Prefixes and suffixes are used to express different verbal categories... The verbal complex consists of a number of prefixes, the root, and a number of suffixes: P1...Pn-R-S1..Sn' with prefix slots for directionals, reflexive/reciprocal, version, conjunctivity, potential, negation, causative and all person markers, and suffix slots for intransitivity, tense, mood and…

evidence_works.detail: The study confirms the published placement (final syllable if heavy, otherwise penult; stress is non-phonemic at the lexical level, p. 55) and finds that stressed vowels have higher F0 in all seven speakers, greater intensity in five, and greater duration in four (non-final syllables); F0 is the most robust correlate. Unstressed vowels at one to four syllables before the stress do not differ from each other in F0 or intensity, so no secondary stress was found, and unstressed /6/ raises gradiently while the stressed /6/ ~ [a:] alternation is categorical.

sources.text: p.145, section 3.1 Stress: "Stress is NOT phonemic. It occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word, except when the following suffixes are added: -ku I, me / -mu you / -na he, she, or definite / -ta we(incl) / -mo already / -pa still. In such cases the stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the word root. For example: 'sapo house, 'sapoku my house, 'ana child, 'anamu your child, 'uma father, 'umata our(incl) father, 'vavu pig, 'vavuna his,her pig, 'peo below, 'peona down below (definite), na'ria have, na'riamo already have."

It occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word, except when the following suffixes are added: -ku 'I, me', -mu 'you', -na 'he, she, or definite', -ta 'we (incl)', -mo 'already', -pa 'still'. In such cases the stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the word root. For example: 'sapo house, 'sapoku my house ... na'ria have, na'riamo already have." (Barr & Barr 1988, PL A-79:145 §3.1)
morph.elicq: "The present study covers the Pekava (Da'a) dialect of Kaili and is based on a corpus of approximately 2,000 words. This data was gathered from September 1979 to May 1980, in the village of Dombu, Marawola Subdistrict (Kecamatan)." (PL A-79:131). The stress section itself (§3.1 p.145) illustrates only with isolated citation forms ('sapo / 'sapoku, 'ana / 'anamu, na'ria / na'riamo); no frame, text or instrumental evidence is mentioned.
morph.stmt: "Da'a, as with many Austronesian (AN) languages, is rich in a variety of bound morphemes marking a number of features... Da'a has two basic forms of bound morphemes: affixes and clitics" (PL A-79:11); per Chart 10 (p.44) the verb is (modal proclitic da)(actor proclitic) FOCUS/MOOD prefix – ASPECT prefixes – causative/transitive/affective/requestive prefixes – ROOT – (lexically limited derivational suffixes -raka etc.) – actor enclitics – modal enclitics -mo/-pa, i.e. derivation and inflection are overwhelmingly prefixal while person (non-focused actor), possessor and perfective marking are enclitic, and noun plurality is by reduplication.

153.tone: Baart 1997 (ch. 5 'Kalami tone') describes five contrastive word melodies — 'high level pitch, high-to-low falling pitch, delayed high-to-low falling pitch, low level pitch, low-to-high rising pitch' (H, HL, H(L), L, LH; p. 41) — not reducible to accent placement ('Kalami, however, has five contrastive patterns', p. 41), and concludes in sec. 5.6 that perceived stress falls at a pitch jump and 'is predictable from the tone patterns' (p. 48); HL words with irregular tone alignment (ˈčočīna, ˈšututur) are marked with a stress mark in the wordlist (p. 49).

154.dq: Stress is independent of length. It falls on the first syllable of a root in Mary's River and Santiam, remaining there when prefixes are added, although in Tualatin and Yoncalla it is often shifted to the prefixed elements. It is generally accompanied by higher (or sometimes lower) pitch, forming what Jacobs calls pitch accent.
154.dloc: Hajda 1976:10, 'The Phonemes of Mary's River Kalapuyan', Stress section; Lewis 2003:3 'High pitch, left-most syllable nucleus on nominal and verbal roots', fn.14 (pp. 63-64) 'stress placement is entirely predictable (on the left-most syllabic nucleus of the root of each noun or verb...)'; StressTyp2 entry (Berman 1990) 'Stress is regularly on the first syllable of a stem.'
154.prule: No fixed position per word length can be given. Primary stress (a high-pitch accent) falls on the first syllabic nucleus of the root and stays there under prefixation (Hajda 1976:10); prefixes — verbal prefix chains and the nominal determiner a(n)- — are unstressed (Lewis 2003:3 fn. 8, ex. 17a-b p. 64); secondary stress on the left-most syllabic nucleus of pronominal/adverbial elements (Lewis 2003 pp. 63-64 fn. 14). quantity-insensitive ("Stress is independent of length") but morphology-anchored, so the position in the word varies with the number of prefix syllables.
154.srule: Secondary stress on the left-most syllabic nucleus of pronominal/adverbial elements (Lewis's third lexical class, often proclitic to the verb), written with a grave accent and less consistent than the root accent of nouns and verbs; no rhythmic secondary stress within noun/verb words is described. Not mentioned in Hajda 1976 (p. 10 'Stress'; MA thesis p. 45 'Suprasegmentals').
154.quote: Stress is independent of length. It falls on the first syllable of a root in Mary's River and Santiam, remaining there when prefixes are added, although in Tualatin and Yoncalla it is often shifted to the prefixed elements. It is generally accompanied by higher (or sometimes lower) pitch, forming what Jacobs calls pitch accent.

154.exq_: Lewis 2003:52: "(In general, nominal and verbal roots are always marked clearly and sharply for stress; such variation would not be found there.) ... (I mark adverbials and demonstratives with grave accents to indicate the variability of their surface stresses.)" fn.14: "secondary stress is on the …
154.tone: Stress is realized as (Jacobs's) 'pitch accent': the root-initial stressed syllable carries higher (sometimes lower) pitch (Hajda 1976:10); Lewis 2003 describes a strong high-pitched accent, predictable on the left-most root nucleus, raised 'some three notes' per Jacobs ca.1930 — no lexical tone contrast is described.

In the 1930's, Jacobs recorded Hudson's speech…
morph.stmt: Predominantly prefixing on both verbs and nouns, with a smaller suffixal layer for valence/objects/aspect: Banks 2007:1, 8 — "Eleven prefix positions and six suffix positions have been identified, with a total of twenty-one prefixes and fifteen suffixes"; "subjects are regularly marked as prefixes and direct and indirect objects as suffixes... 156.dq: 2.17.1. WORD STRESS. Each word is marked by primary stress on the first syllable. ... I now believe that there is only one phonological rule and that this rule places primary stress on the first syllable of the word. Other secondary stresses may occur but their appearance seems to be sporadic, being determined by tempo and by hesitations and the like.
156.dloc: Blake 1979:25-26, (opened; in); StressTyp2 entry (Blake 1969:16-17) "Main stress is word initial... Word final syllables are unstressed."
156.srule: Optional and not rule-governed (Blake 1979:26): secondary stresses 'may occur but their appearance seems to be sporadic', depending on tempo and hesitation, and 'in fluent speech they hardly occur at all'; when present they normally fall on the first syllable of a non-word-initial polysyllabic morpheme (ṯúar-kùṉa), spaced by one or two unstressed syllables; on the 2nd or 4th syllable only under contrastive stress.

morph.stmt: As described by Blake, Kalkatungu inflection and derivation are exclusively suffixal: 'nominals in AGENT (A) function are marked by a suffix (-t̪u or -ŋku)' (§3.1 p.27), chapter 4 is 'Tense and aspect suffixes', bound pronouns are 'suffixed to' the verb or to the particles a-/ku- (§3.3), and all Ch.5 function morphemes (-jan, -it̪i, -ɲcir, -wati, -mia, -puni, -ma, -jat̪i, -ti, -nti, -ɲcama...) are suffixes; the only mention of prefixation in the grammar is that the complementiser-plus-pronoun laa 'in rapid speech... may be prefixed to the verb as la' (§3.4 p.39), and the 'definitiser' pa is a free demonstrative (§5.10.2).

157.prule: Primary stress falls regularly on the final syllable of the word (Saelzer 1976:134 §2.1.4); when a noun is suffixed the primary stress may move to the new final syllable or stay on the stem-final syllable, and sentence-finally the suffix takes the stress.

corr.detail: StressTyp2 codes initial primary stress; the description it cites places main stress without exception on the root-initial syllable with unstressed prefixes, so the position in the word depends on morphological structure (prefixed words are not initial-stressed). ev.text: Roots are disyllabic and main stress is without exception on the root-initial syllable. Only CVV and CV syllables can bear stress, CVC syllables are never stressed. Prefixes, suffixes and almost all clitics are unstressed.

The facultative closing oe [the paragogic /u/] does not count as a syllable — (wátar or wátaroe).' [For the exclusively disyllabic Kambera roots, penult-of-stem = initial-of-root, so Wielenga and Klamer state the same fact.]

Main stress falls without exception on the root-initial syllable of the prosodic word, where the prosodic word explicitly contains the affixes (Klamer 2005:710, 712; van der Hulst & Klamer 1997:121). Prefixes and proclitics are word-internal unstressed pretonic syllables; suffixes, enclitics, and paragogic /u/ are unstressed and stress-neutral; compounds bear word stress on the second member (Klamer 2005:731-732). 158.quote: Main stress is always on the root-initial syllable (see below). ... Kambera has three syllable types: CVV (where VV is a long vowel, a diphthong or a vowel sequence), CV, and CVC. Kambera does not allow closed syllables at the surface, i.e. CVC syllables are only found lexically. Roots are disyllabic and main stress is without exception on the root-initial syllable. Only CVV and CV syllables can bear stress, CVC syllables are never stressed. Prefixes, suffixes and almost all clitics are unstressed.

morph.rootq: Csató 2012 p.37: "The stress pattern is similar to the normal Turkic one. The stressed syllable is normally the last syllable in the word. ... When a suffix that cannot carry stress, as for instance the negation suffix -MA, the preceding syllable is stressed, e.g. anlamadym [ɑn'lɑmɑdïm] 'I didn't understand (it)'. Compounds are stressed on their first element, e.g. biugiuń ['bjygjʉnj] 'today'. This pattern is valid also in compounds which are today not analysable any more ... and in some verbs including a causative suffix, e.g. siekirmia ['sjekjirmjæ] 'to jump/to dance'." and p.38: "The instrumental suffix is not accented."…
morph.elicq: Csató 2012 gives no statement of how stress was determined; the article only fixes notation (p.35: "Word accent is denoted by ' in front of the accented syllable, e.g. kieliad'liar [kje'ljædjljær] 'they come'") and supplies accent marks on isolated citation words plus one transcribed prayer sentence (p.36 "[tɑ'bu e'tjæbjizj tenjrji'gjæ] ... [bolušlu'γu yčjʉnj bjizjgjæ]"). The supplementary source Kowalski 1929 marks non-final stress throughout dictated connected texts: p.lxxiii "eine sorgfältige Durchschnittsaussprache eines gebildeten Karaimen ... durch mehrere Textaufnahmen nach dem Diktat von verschiedenen Individuen".
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing (no prefixes or proclitics in either source; 79 text tokens: 64 suffix morphs, 0 prefix morphs). Csató 2012 p.37: "Karaim has a synthetic morphological structure employing numerous morphosyntactic categories with very generalised contents. The nominal paradigm includes singular and plural forms, seven case suffixes, and five possessive suffixes." Kowalski 1929 and Zajączkowski 1932 (cited by Csató p.35) describe the morphology entirely as "nominal and verbal suffixes".

160.srule: Secondary stress on every odd-numbered non-final syllable after the first (3rd, 5th...); the final syllable is usually unstressed (apocope dialects such as Ludic may keep a final secondary stress); in compounds the secondary stress falls on the first syllable of the second component. StressTyp2 (after Hayes 1995: 279 / Leskinen 1984) adds that the secondaries 'may sometimes be shifted to every third syllable'.
160.quote: Word stress in Karelian is constant. The primary stress always falls on the first syllable (pái-men / pái-moi ’a shepherd’), with the exception of some late Russian borrowings, in which the primary stress may sometimes fall on other syllables. In the standard varieties of Karelian stress can only be on the first syllable. The Karelian language always features secondary stress, which usually falls on every odd syllable of a compound noun, excluding the last one

160.sec_quote: The Karelian language always features secondary stress, which usually falls on every odd syllable of a compound noun, excluding the last one, while the second and even syllables remain unstressed (méč-čä-níek-ka / méč-čy-níek-ku 'a hunter'). A primary and secondary stress cannot, therefore, fall on consecutive syllables. The alternation of stressed and unstressed syllables gives Karelian its rhythmic nature. The final syllable is usually unstressed.

161.dq: The first syllable of a word always carries the heaviest stress (indicated by ´), and weaker stresses (`) occur on the alternate following syllables. In three syllable words, however, the weak stress on the third syllable is often omitted. Examples are: há.ta 'road', ká.ro.rac 'cloud' and sá.ma.rì.e.kac 'he exerted himself'.
161.dloc: Flierl & Strauss (eds.) 1977, Kâte Dictionary (PL C-41), front matter 'Stress Placement', p. xx
161.prule: Primary (heaviest) stress always falls on the first syllable of the word; diphthongs count as single vowels for stress placement, and a stressed diphthong carries the stress on its first (syllabic) vowel.
161.srule: Weaker stresses fall on alternate syllables after the initial primary stress (3rd, 5th...); in three-syllable words the weak stress on the third syllable is often omitted, and no example marks a weak stress on a word-final syllable. Object-marking suffixes carry a weak stress on their first syllable, so with a trisyllabic verb root the stresses fall on the 1st and 4th syllables (má.ma.kâc.jò.pa.wec) instead of 1st and 3rd; compound verbs vary between one heavy stress and two with speech rate.
161.quote: The first syllable of a word always carries the heaviest stress (indicated by ´), and weaker stresses (`) occur on the alternate following syllables. In three syllable words, however, the weak stress on the third syllable is often omitted. Examples are: há.ta 'road', ká.ro.rac 'cloud' and sá.ma.rì.e.kac 'he exerted himself'. It has been noted that the diphthongs function as single vowels in the determination of stress placement. When a diphthong is stressed, it is the first vowel (i.e., the syllabic vowel) which carries the stress.
161.idn: Kâte, Wemo (= Wena) dialect — the mission/church standard: the dictionary (a revision of Keysser 1925) is restricted to the Wena [Wemo] dialect, which 'is spoken today throughout the greater Kâte area'; the sound-system and stress description is McElhanon's, written for Wemo speakers' distinctions; data: Finschhafen…
161.exq_: The only deviation from the normal word stress pattern occurs when the verb root has three syllables so that the resulting stresses are on the first and fourth syllables rather than on the first and third syllables as in má.ma.kâc.jò.pa.wec 'he loathed them' [p. xxii; weak stress only]

Although these have not been investigated in depth, some preliminary observations are in order.' (p.xxi); speech-rate observations imply some listening to connected speech: 'In slow speech, speakers frequently insert a juncture between the elements in the compound and this results in two contiguous heavy stresses ... In rapid speech, however, this juncture drops out and the result is a single heavy stress with weaker stresses as in the normal pattern' (p.xxi).

tn.quote: Jabêm distinguishes seven vowel positions, plus high or low tone (pitch) at each position (Bradshaw and Czobor 2003: 2–3). … In sum, the Kâte and Jabêm vowel systems have not converged. (However, Sio’s six-vowel system matches that of Kâte.) Jabêm developed phonemic tone for internal reasons, but no tonal distinctions are found in Kâte. … Neither language has adopted the most distinctive phonological features of the other. Jabêm’s tonal distinctions have not penetrated into Kâte, nor have Kâte’s coarticulated labiovelar stops been borrowed into Jabêm.
tn.cite: Bradshaw, Joel. 2016. Papuan Kâte and Austronesian Jabêm: Long contact, little convergence. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 34(1): 59-76.
tn.note: No tone: unlike neighbouring Jabêm with its high/low tone contrast, Kâte has no tonal distinctions.

morph.src: Li, Paul Jen-kuei & Shigeru Tsuchida. 2006. Kavalan Dictionary. Language and Linguistics Monograph Series A-19. Taipei: Institute of Linguistics, Academia Sinica. (Introduction pp. 1-42: phonology, morphology with full affix inventory, syntax; Texts pp. 43-62: four interlinear glossed narrative texts; dictionary body used for root analyses of the disputed stems.)
morph.rootq: "Stress falls on the final syllable. The penultimate vowel is phonetically long, especially preceding a single consonant, e.g. /sunis/[su:nís] 'child'." (§2.1.1 p.3); "All four vowels may receive stress, specifically on the final syllable." (§2.1.2 p.3). The statement is about the word-final syllable with no reference to root or affix; the authors' own phonetic forms show stress landing on a suffix, e.g. qaniyauan [qanijau:án] 'they, Loc' (p.4), and vowel loss 'especially in an unstressed syllable' (p.9).
morph.elicq: No method statement. The stress claim is illustrated only with phonetic transcriptions of single citation words: "Stress falls on the final syllable ... e.g. /sunis/[su:nís] 'child'" (p.3), "suRna [so:ná] 'snow'" (p.2), "qulu [qo:dú] 'to support'" (p.3); the introduction refers readers to Li (1982) and Moriguchi (1983) 'discussion of vowel length and accent in Kavalan' (p.2) for the phonology.
morph.stmt: "Prefixation predominates. There are only two productive infixes: (1) -um- or -m- 'Agent-focus', phonologically conditioned; and (2) -in- or -n- as variants of ni-... In addition to the bound genitive pronouns, -ku, -su, -na, etc., there are only three other suffixes: (1) -a 'irrealis Patient-focus marker'; (2) -an 'Locative-focus, nominalizer'; and (3) -i 'imperative, Patient-focus'. The lack of *-en is notable." (§3.1 p.12). The prefix inventory runs to c. 60 items (pp.14-23); aspect/tense =ti, =pa, relativizer =ay, question =i, imperative =ka and nominative pronouns are enclitics (p.12-13).

vlen.q: Stress in Kavalan is not attracted to non-final vowel-glide sequences. For example, qawpir ‘sweet potato’ is realized as [qaw.píχ], not *[qáw.piχ] ... Coda consonants can also not attract stress to non-final syllables. ... In neither case is stress attracted…

evidence_works.detail: Final (ultima) stress stated as regular, with the semivowel analysis (/y, w/ phonemic, so nearly every word ends in a consonant) making it exceptionless; no exceptions listed, no secondary stress mentioned, no tone mentioned anywhere in the chapter. Weight is not invoked for stress placement; the only length remark is phonetic: 'A vowel other than /ə/ is phonetically long on the penultimate syllable unless it is followed by a consonant cluster' (p. 285), i.e. pretonic lengthening, not stress-attracting weight. p. 287: /i, u, a/ 'occur... in the stressed syllable'; /ə/ 'may not occur word-fina

163.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables counting leftward from the final (primary) stress: /'i.pe."ʔyi/ 'pato pequeno', /i.'pe.yu."ʔu/ 'pato grande', /'ja.ʔwa."run/ 'onça preta' (Weiss 1998, who frames the strongest stress as utterance-final before pause). Not mentioned in Souza 2004 §2.3.7 or Dobson 2005 §7.

morph.elicq: No statement ties the stress rule to a particular kind of evidence. Dobson 1988/2005 Prefácio p.4: 'A análise descrita nos artigos deste volume baseia-se em dados coletados nas três localidades acima citadas, durante o período de 1966-1977.' Souza 2004 p.20-21 describes general elicitation sessions with two male speakers in Campinas (1997, 1999) plus data from Dobson marked (R.D.); her stress examples (33)-(34) are isolated derived words/phrases (/e.it/+/i/ -> /e.i.ri/ 'suco de mel'; /ʔok/+/ipe/ -> /ʔo.gi.pe/ 'para casa') with no frame or instrumental evidence mentioned.
morph.stmt: Mixed but person-prefixing / TAM-suffixing: Dobson 1997 p.38 'na língua kayabi, o indicador de pessoa se encontra como prefixo no verbo... e o tempo está indicado por uma palavra separada que ocorre no fim da oração'; verb template Dobson 1988/2005 Figura 6 p.27 '(n-) suj/obj radical (aspecto) (-i)' [declarative], 'suj/obj radical (aspecto) tn (-e'em)' [narrative]. 164.qtr: 5. INTENSITY [= stress]. Stress is not predictable in phonological terms. Grammatically, it normally falls on the last syllable of the stem of the word. /pu'nu/ 'bad' /pu'nu-řɛ/ 'a little bad (diminutive)'

dqtr.text: 5. INTENSITY [STRESS]. Intensity (stress) is not predictable in phonological terms. Grammatically, it normally occurs on the last syllable of the theme (stem) of the word. /pu'nu/ 'bad/evil' /pu'nu-řɛ/ 'little bad one (diminutive)'

164.dq: 5. INTENSIDADE. A Intensidade não é predizível em termos fonológicos. Gramaticalmente, ocorre normalmente na última sílaba do tema da palavra. /pu'nu/ 'mal' /pu'nu-řɛ/ 'mauzinho'
164.dloc: Stout & Thomson 1974:163 §5 (etnolinguistica.org scan, suffix glyph read as -řɛ on by the owner review)
164.prule: No count-computable rule rides: primary stress falls on the final syllable of the STEM ("normalmente na última sílaba do tema da palavra"), so the surface position is a function of morphological parse (number of post-stem suffix syllables), not of syllable count. Descriptive rule of record for the errata: stem-final stress, quantity-insensitive, word-level, hedged by "normalmente".
164.srule: Not mentioned in Stout & Thomson 1974 (§5 'Intensidade' p. 163; whole article pp. 153-176 read; note 2 p. 176: the analysis does not go beyond the syllable). Later statement, compounds only: every subordinate (non-final) stem of a compound keeps a secondary stress, primary stress on the last stem ([ˌɾɔmˈnɔ] 'lanterna' < rop + no; [ˌpaɾiˈkʌ] 'calçado' < pari + kà) — Salanova & Nikulin 2020:66 fn. 12; no rhythmic secondary stress is described for simple words (simple stems are mono- or sesquisyllabic, pp. 69-70).

Nominalizations and aspect. PhD dissertation, MIT.
morph.rootq: Stout & Thomson 1974:163 §5: 'INTENSIDADE. A Intensidade não é predizível em termos fonológicos. Gramaticalmente, ocorre normalmente na última sílaba do tema da palavra. /pu'nu/ 'mal', /pu'nu-ře/ 'mauzinho'.' Costa 2015:45-46 (§1.3): 'O acento primário incide, com maior frequência, sobre a sílaba final da palavra. O conjunto de formas excepcionais é formado por: (1) termos derivados por meio da adição de sufixos extramétricos e que, portanto, não 'atraem' o acento e (2) formas derivadas pela adição de uma 'vogal eco' ou 'vogal previsível'. ... [puˈnu] 'ruim, feio', [puˈnuɾɛ] 'ruim, feio' (atenuativo). Em (e), acima, temos como exemplo de sufixo extramétrico o Atenuativo -/ɾɛ/.'
morph.elicq: Neither source says what kind of evidence the stress statement rests on. Stout & Thomson 1974:153: 'As autoras recolheram os dados na aldéia de Porori no Parque Nacional do Xingú, durante várias visitas feitas de janeiro de 1965 a fevereiro de 1970 ... A análise feita teve como informantes homens e mulheres de todas as idades e algumas crianças de 10 anos em diante.' Costa 2015:24 (§0.5): 'A metodologia ... consistiu em coleta de dados elicitados, seguindo questionários pré-elaborados ..., mas também de coleta de relatos, conversas e outros atos de fala naturais. Os dados elicitados se constituem de listas de palavras sobre vocabulário básico ... frases e sentenças com foco em aspectos…
morph.stmt: Costa 2015:127: 'verbos transitivos, intransitivos nominalizados, nomes relativos e posposições são as únicas classes de palavras flexionáveis, sendo as demais classes invariáveis' -- and that inflection is entirely PREFIXAL (person markers i-/a-/ku- plus the 'prefixos relacionais' R1 j-/ɲ-/ʤ-/Ø- and R2 Ø-/ku-, ch.III), as is the causative ɔ- and middle aj-; derivation is SUFFIXAL (nominalizers -m/-n/-j/-ɾV, -ʤwəj, -ʤʌ; attenuative -ɾɛ, intensive -ti), while tense-aspect, mood, negation, number, and interrogation are carried by free particles (na/ʤa, ɾãʔã, ket, mẽ, djə). Net profile: light inflectional prefixing on the stem, derivational suffixing, otherwise isolating/particle-based.

contra.head: A dissenting description, reported second-hand
contra.detail: Known only from the report in McCollum & Chen 2021: 291; none of the four dissenting works has been obtained, so the dissent is unconfirmed. Two positions: a word-initial stress accent plus a word-final pitch accent (Kirchner 1998), and no word-level stress, only phrase-level prominence (Dzhunisbekov; Abuov; Vajda). Their own one-speaker study finds no final pitch accent (p. 293) and states (p. 294): 'we do not extrapolate to argue more concretely for either the existence or stress or its placement in Kazakh'. The first-hand descriptions held put regular stress word-finally (Dotton & Wagner [2018]; Özçelik 2015, analysing Kazakh as a weight-sensitive iamb, 'still mostly final', p. 188).

165.caution: McCollum & Chen 2021 (one speaker) draw no conclusion on stress placement and report dissenting descriptions in print: initial stress accent plus final pitch accent (Kirchner 1998) and no word-level stress (Dzhunisbekov 1980, 1987; Abuov 1994; Vajda 1994), not yet read. Özçelik 2015 analyses the system as a weight-sensitive iamb with heavy syllables attracting stress in some roots.

morph.rootq: §2.5 pp.14-15: "Kazakh lexical stress is typically syllable-final. ... Morphologically complex words consistently place the stress on the final syllable, even in increasing levels of complexity [bala, bala-lar, bala-lar-ym, bala-lar-ymyz, bala-lar-ymyz-ǵa]. However, certain verbal tenses permit for stress on the penultimate syllable. These tenses include the imperative mood, the habitual past, the indirect past, and the optative. Additionally, word-final clitics in Kazakh (question particles, agreement suffixes) do not take stress, moving instead the center of stress to the penultimate syllable." Also §3.4.7 p.29: "unlike many of the case forms, the instrumental case is not stressed…
morph.elicq: §2.5 p.14: "Kazakh lexical stress is typically syllable-final. (36) jumyrtqa 'egg' (37) qazaqstan 'Kazakhstan' (38) áke 'father'" — the section gives isolated citation words, one morphological build-up series and three sentence examples with grave-accent stress marks, but nowhere states how stress was determined (no mention of speakers, recordings, frames or measurements).
morph.stmt: §3 p.17: "The morphology of the Kazakh language can be categorized as an agglutinative system that exclusively uses suffixes for both derivational and inflectional processes." (The only pre-root grammatical material in the grammar is the free superlative particle eń 'most' and emphatic partial reduplication qap-qara 'very black', §3.8.3 p.53.)

tn.quote: Dzhunisbekov (1987) has demonstrated that Kazakh and other Turkic languages with synharmony are typologically distinct from intonation languages, such as English, as well as from tone languages, such as Chinese. ... Although synharmony does not operate across word boundaries, it interacts with the prosodic system of Kazakh by allowing stress to assume a predominantly syntactic role in the language. Languages with synharmony have rhythmic stress; they differ fundamentally from both stress/intonation languages and tone languages.

tn.note: Kazakh classed as neither a tone nor a stress/intonation language: synharmony defines the word, stress is phrasal (rhythmic-group-final), following Dzhunisbekov; no pitch/tone analysis given.

166.dq: Stress always falls on the final syllable. Only some words that have been taken from Malay are an exception to this rule. When suffixes are added to a word the stress falls on the suffix that is the final syllable of the derived word. In words with more than two syllables the first syllable is also stressed, but the final syllable bears the strongest stress. (Geurtjens 1922)

166.srule: None per Travis 1990:7: 'Kei phonological words are rhythm groups which contain exactly one stressed syllable (vowel)' (3-4-syllable words transcribed with one final stress and a reduced initial vowel, e.g. [náf.tal.wa'ang]). Earlier report, Geurtjens 1921:7: in words of more than two syllables the first syllable is also pronounced with more emphasis, the heaviest stress remaining on the final syllable.
166.quote: Kei phonological words are rhythm groups which contain exactly one stressed syllable (vowel). Phonological word stress carries higher pitch, loudness, and longer duration than unstressed syllables. Since grammatical word breaks always distinguish the two types of phonological words, word stress is not phonemic for the Kei language. There are two types of phonological words: I. (S)'S -- common grammatical words: ultimate stress II. (S)'SS -- multiple grammatical units: non-ultimate stress ... The majority of grammatical words are type I with ultimate stress.

morph.stmt: van Engelenhoven 2021 (abstract, p.399): Ewaw has 'seventeen derivational prefixes, and four derivational suffixes', all petrified — 'Reduplication is the only productive morphological device in Ewaw' — while productive inflection consists of pronominal subject proclitics + prefixes on verbs (o=m-tetan '2SG=2SG-cut') and single-consonant possessor suffixes on inalienable nouns (lima-ng 'my hand') beside preposed possessive proclitics for alienables (nung=buk 'my book'); so bound marking before the root (person proclitic+prefix, derivational prefixes, reduplicative prefix) outnumbers the small set of non-syllabic suffixes (-ng/-m/-n/-d/-b/-r; -k/-t/-n/-ng) and post-verbal enclitics.

morph.stmt: No grammar of Kela exists, so there is no author's summary; what the phonological sources document is prefixal: verbs take pronominal subject prefixes and (productively in Lambu, fossilized in Southern Kala) realis prefixes before the stem - 'there is a form of consonant voicing harmony between pronominal prefixes and realis prefixes (irrealis is unmarked in Lambu)' (Ransdell-Green 2022:42; 'Kala ostensibly lacks vowel-initial verb stems', fn.5) - and kin-term possessors are a preposed 'qualifying affix' (aŋ-azi 'his father', Collier & Collier 1975:150); the only post-root material seen is an unanalysed plural (guɾuwa/guɾuwaɾa) and a noun qualifier (moa-lilina).

167.cfw: The antepenultimate rule (initial in words of up to three syllables) rests only on Collier and Collier's 1975 tentative statement of the Apoze village dialect, whereas Johnson 1994 gives penultimate stress for the Kui dialect and Ransdell-Green's 2022 phonology of Southern Kala finds stress usually penultimate, always so in disyllables, and antepenultimate only in certain longer words with variation between speakers, so the record stands for Apoze but not for the language as a whole.

tn.quote: Each Ket monosyllabic stem, when pronounced in isolation, is characterized by one of four contrastive suprasegmental entities; their relevant phonetic basis is not absolute or relative tone-height, but rather contour and phonation. ... their distinctive features ... are only relevant as long as the tone-bearing unit/lexeme remains an isolated monosyllable; upon suffixation ... all of these features are cancelled, giving way to one of two disyllabic contours, which perceptively resemble patterns of accentuation ... The domain of Ket tones is thus the leftmost two syllables of a word.
tn.cite: Georg, Stefan. 2007. A Descriptive Grammar of Ket (Yenisei-Ostyak). Part 1: Introduction, Phonology, Morphology. Folkestone: Global Oriental.
tn.note: Four contour/phonation tonemes on isolated monosyllables, lost on affixation; longer words take one of two pitch-accent-like contours (5th/6th 'tone', ásel: àsel) on syllables 1-2; F0 from Werner.

contra.head: An 1857 Koibal grammar treats stress on a long penult as only apparent, against the 1975 grammar's 'long vowels are always stressed'
contra.detail: Castrén's Koibalische Sprachlehre is an impressionistic description of the Koibal dialect (no procedure stated). Castrén holds that a long penult before a short final only seems to take the accent: 'Ist die Endsilbe aber kurz und die vorletzte lang, so neigt sich das Tongewicht sehr schwach auf die Endsilbe und es kommt dem Ohre fast vor, als rücke der Accent auf die vorletzte Silbe zurück. Doch ist dieses Zurückrücken nur scheinbar, denn bei einer angestrengteren Aussprache wird auch in diesem Fall die Endsilbe betont.' (§32, p. 10). He also separates accent from quantity: 'Demnach können auch im Koibalischen sowohl betonte als unbetonte Silben sowohl lang als kurz sein.' (§31, p. 10).

qtr.text: § 49. One of the syllables in a word is stressed. Khakas, like all Turkic languages, has dynamic (force) stress [...] 1. In two-, three- and four-syllable root words with short vowels the stress usually falls on the last syllable: хызыл 'red', хузух 'nut', хузурух 'tail', чистек 'berry', палтырган 'angelica', харагай 'pine'. 2. In monosyllabic words the vowels correspond in intensity to the stressed vowels of polysyllabic words. 3. Long vowels of the stem (root) are always stressed, regardless of their place in the word. Cf. e.g. чоорған 'blanket' — чорга 'ambler'; хазаа 'cattle yard' — хаза …

169.dq: § 49. Один из слогов в слове является ударным. ... 1. В двусложных, трех- и четырехсложных корневых словах с краткими гласными ударение обычно падает на последний слог: хызыл 'красный', хузух 'орех', хузурух 'хвост', чистек 'ягода', палтырган 'дягиль', харагай 'сосна'.
169.prule: Stress as a rule falls on the last syllable of the word: root words with short vowels are stressed on the final syllable and the stress moves onto plural, case, causative, past-tense affixes and restrictive particles as they are added. Stated conditions: long root vowels are always stressed wherever they stand; verbal negation affixes keep the stress when further affixes follow; interrogative particles never take the stress.
169.srule: Polysyllabic words have a secondary stress besides the main stress: a long stem vowel that loses the main stress to a stress-taking affix keeps its length and carries secondary stress (чоохтабинча, саасханнар, хазаада, чоохтабаан); no positional rhythmic rule is given.
169.quote: § 49. Один из слогов в слове является ударным. Для хакасского языка, как и для всех тюркских языков, характерно силовое ударение [...] 1. В двусложных, трех- и четырехсложных корневых словах с краткими гласными ударение обычно падает на последний слог: хызыл ‘красный’ хузух ‘орех’, хузурух ‘хвост’, чистек ‘ягода’, палтырган ‘дягиль’, харагай ‘сосна’. 2. В односложных словах гласные соотвегствуют [sic] по интенсивности ударным гласным многосложных слов. 3. Долгие гласные основы (корня) всегда ударные, независимо от места их в слове. Ср. например, чоорған ‘одеяло’ — чорга ‘иноходец’; хазаа ‘ско…

169.idn: modern general/literary Khakas ('общенародный хакасский язык'), normed mainly on the Kachin and Sagay dialects; §49 adds that dialect features often shift the stress and §§2-7 survey the Sagay, Kachin, Kyzyl, Shor dialects separately

morph.elicq: Baskakov (ed.) 1975 §49, pp.44–45: «В многосложных словах кроме основного ударения имеется второстепенное ударение. Поэтому иногда трудно бывает уловить на слух ударный слог в слове. … Вопрос об ударении в хакасском языке пока еще мало разработан, он требует всестороннего экспериментального исследования.» (All supporting forms are cited as isolated words, e.g. хызыл, хузурух, чоохтабинча; no frame or instrumental procedure is described — the description is auditory/impressionistic.)
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing agglutinative morphology: «Аффикс — это отдельный звук или комплекс звуков, фонетически зависимый от корня, за которым он следует» (Baskakov 1975 §51, p.47); derivational, then form-building, then inflectional suffixes close the word («словоизменяющие являются замыкающими: тоғыс-чы-лар-ға», §51 p.49; мал-ҷы-лар-ыбыс-таң-ар, тоғын-ғла-п-чат-хан-нар, p.52); the only pre-posed grammatical elements are free particles (иң ‘самый’, сах ‘точно’, §266) and the interrogative/limitative particles are postposed enclitics. Maltseva & Sultrekova 2023: 'Khakas syntax is typically for Turkic … Left-branching verb-final sentences are the rule.'

excx.exc_elsewhere_quote: § 24. Ударение в слове экспираторное, фиксированное на последнем слоге. В многосложных словах—двухполюсное, т. е. состоит, как правило, из слабого на одном из первых слогов и сильного—на последнем слоге, напр.: пабàзынáң ’от своего отца’. Однако, в зависимости от характера словообразовательных и словоизменительных аффиксов, ударение не всегда переходит на последний из них в слове. Так, в отрицательной форме глагола главное ударение обычно сохраняет свою первоначальную позицию на последнем…

169.sec_rule: Stated: polysyllabic words carry a secondary stress besides the main stress; the placement given is that a long root vowel which cedes the main stress to a stress-taking affix keeps its length and bears secondary stress (чо̀охтабинча́, са̀асханна́р, хаза̀ада́, чо̀охтабаа́н); placement in polysyllables without long vowels is not specified.
169.sec_quote: В многосложных словах кроме основного ударения имеется второстепенное ударение. [...] в словах с долгим гласным в основе при прибавлении аффикса, на который переходит ударение, эти доглие гласные из ударных превращаются в неударные и произносятся с сохранением своей долготы, как гласные второстепенного ударения. Например, чоохтабинча ‘не говорит’, саасханнар ‘сороки’, хазаада ‘во дворе’ [...]
169.sec_cite: Grammatika xakasskogo jazyka, ed. N. A. Baskakov (phonetics chapter by D. I. Chankov). Moskva: Nauka, 1975.

secx.sec_quote_tr: In polysyllabic words there is, besides the main stress, a secondary stress. [...] in words with a long vowel in the stem, when an affix onto which the stress passes is added, these long vowels turn from stressed into unstressed and are pronounced keeping their length, as vowels of secondary stress. For example, чоохтабинча 'does not speak', саасханнар 'magpies', хазаада 'in the yard' [...]

PhD thesis, Deccan College Postgraduate and Research Institute / University of Poona (later published 1985 as 'Khasi: a descriptive analysis'). Open on Shodhganga, hdl.handle.net/10603/258094. morph.rootq: Nagaraja 1977, Introduction p. iv: 'In this study suprasegmental features like stress, intonation are not analysed.' (The phonology, Part I pp. 1-51, has no word-stress section; only word and syllable juncture §1.5.) Nagaraja 1990 Khasi Phonetic Reader p. 26 likewise only: 'Duration is phonemic for vowels. Also stress and pitch are distinctive contextually—stress is for emphasis and pitch for intonation.'
morph.elicq: No stress description in the source used. The project's E=RIGHT coding rests on Rabel 1961:30 as relayed by StressTyp2 and Schiering & van der Hulst 2010:594: 'Rabel's (1961: 30) observation that Khasi words, at least in isolation, have word-final primary accent' — i.e. isolated words; Rabel 1961 itself is lending-restricted on archive.org and was not re-read here.
morph.stmt: Nagaraja (Introduction p. iv): 'In Khasi very little of morphology is found... Under the latter part whatever little morphology there is, is described.' What bound morphology exists is prefixal — causative pɨn-, collective/reciprocal ya-, pretentive leʔmɨn-, inclinative sam- (§3.1.1: 'Causative verbs are derived by prefixing pɨn- to the verbs'), nominalisers noŋ-, jɨŋ- (§2.1.2.1: 'The process involved in this is prefixation of derivative markers to the verbs') — and all inflection-like categories (gender/number articles u/ka/ki/i, tense la/-n, aspect daŋ, modals, negation -m/ɨm) are preposed particles or clitics ('Except for completive marker, all others occur before a verb', §3.3 p.89)…

Stress is distributed by syllable type, not count: every full (major) syllable is stressed, every reduced-shape syllable (presyllables CV+, CrV+, CVN+, CrVN+, vowel reduced to /ə/; Nacaskul's minor syllables with rime-restricted vowels) is unstressed. 171.dq: Minor disyllables consist of an unstressed presyllable of shape CV+, CrV+, CVN+, or CrVN+, followed by a stressed syllable. ... Major disyllables consist of two stressed syllables in close juncture. Most such words are compounds; some, however, are morphologically simple
171.dloc: Huffman 1970:11, re-quoted from the note on the cited source (verbatim quotes transcribed); the domain ruling there: "Domain: word. Both treatments sit in word-structure chapters and quantify over words ("Word Structure", "Cambodian words"); no phrasal-domain statement anywhere." StressTyp2 entry (Huffman 1970:10) banks the parallel sentence; entry (Gorgoniyev 1966:31): "Stress in disyllabic words is final."; entry (Jacob 1968:14): "The first syllable of many disyllabic words lacks stress with respect to the second."
171.heavy: Stressed = full ('major') syllable C1(C2)(C3)V1(V2)(C4) where 'short vowels are always followed by a consonant in stressed syllables' (i.e. CVV(C) or CVC with a full vowel); unstressed = presyllable of shape CV+, CrV+, CVN+, CrVN+ whose vowel is 'usually reduced to /ə/' (Huffman). Nacaskul: minor syllable (Cv, Crv with short vowel; or CvN with vowel restricted to /ɔ/, /ù/, /ɨ̀ə/) 'weakly stressed'; major syllable 'bearing stronger stress'; two major syllables = 'equal stress on each'.
171.dflt: not applicable: every word ends in a full (major) syllable, which takes the primary stress
171.prule: The word-final syllable is always a full (major) syllable and is stressed in every transcribed example, carrying the acute at all lengths 2-6 (/kəkáay/, /phìəsáa/, /sdúəc-sdáəŋ/, /thò̆əm+mə+dáa/, /pút+tə+sáh+snáa/, /ríəc+rò̆ət+tháa+phi+báal/, /wi+cáa+rə+náq+kə+tháa/); elsewhere in the same volume Huffman states '(A stressed syllable is any syllable in isolation, or any word-final syllable.)' (1970:104, exercise 80). Huffman distinguishes only stressed vs unstressed and never uses 'primary' ('Major disyllables consist of two stressed syllables in close juncture'); final PRIMACY (one main stress, final) is the reading of Gorgoniyev 1966:31 'Stress in disyllabic words is final' and Jacob 1968:14 (StressTyp2 carried quotes) plus the final never being grave-marked; Nacaskul 1978:189 gives two major syllables 'equal stress on each'.
171.srule: Non-final full (major) syllables are also stressed; reduced presyllables are not. 'Major disyllables consist of two stressed syllables in close juncture' (incl. morphologically simple /sìəwphɨ́w/ 'book', /phìəsáa/ 'language'); polysyllabic loans 'tend to conform... to... alternation of an unstressed with a stressed syllable', Huffman's transcriptions marking 2-3 stresses per word by syllable make-up (/pút+tə+sáh+snáa/ 1011, /ríəc+ròə̆t+tháa+phi+báal/ 11101, /wi+cáa+rə+náq+kə+tháa/ 010101). Huffman does not rank the stresses (acute vs grave on non-final syllables unexplained in this volume); Nacaskul 1978:189 gives two major syllables 'equal stress on each'.

However, the language has borrowed a great many words from Pali and Sanskrit, with the result that there are now many polysyllables, especially in literary and educated usage. In all cases, however, the main stress falls on the last syllable of the word: /bət/ "to close", /tŭənlee/ "river", /meʔkəraa/ "January", /paccobɑnphiəp/ "current events." In polysyllables stressed and unstressed syllables alternate, e.g. /phooceniyəthaan/ "restaurant." In most compounds (words made up of two or more other words), each component keeps its stress pattern.'…
morph.elicq: No method statement; the stress rule (P.4 p.10) is illustrated only with isolated citation forms ('/bət/ "to close", /tŭənlee/ "river", /meʔkəraa/ "January" ...'), while P.5-P.6 discuss stress inside sentence intonation contours and casual connected speech ('the more casual the circumstances, the more reduction is likely to take place in unstressed syllables ... so that in some dialects all that may remain of an unstressed syllable is the initial consonant and a reduced vowel /ə/', P.6 p.12). The sketch is a pedagogical description based on work with the informant Kem Sos ('an excellent linguistic informant', Foreword) and on Huffman 1967; no instrumental data.
morph.stmt: Ehrman I.3 pp.13-14: 'Cambodian may be typed as an isolating language, which means that it makes most of its grammatical distinctions by means of word-order rather than by means of affixes and changes within words. Native Khmer words may include prefixes, suffixes, and infixes which change the part of speech... or which change the root meaning of a word without changing its grammatical function. However, while the patterns of affixation are complex, the affixes are seldom used in new combinations'; V.3.2 p.59: 'Complex verbs are formed by prefixation and infixation... the affixes are not productive, though some are very widespread' -- i.e. exclusively prefixing/infixing derivational…

172.exq_: A main syllable is the syllable that occurs alone as a monosyllabic word or as the last syllable of a disyllabic or trisyllabic word. It is always stressed. Its vowel has full quality. The presyllable, the syllable that comes before the main syllable, is always unstressed and very weak.

morph.elicq: §1.5 pp.4-5: 'The phonological analysis is based on the last two informants who are 22 and 24 years respectively. The syntactic analysis is based on the informant elicitation and the text materials of about 30 hours of speech recorded from people in the village regardless of sex, age and occupation differences.' The stress section (§2.5) gives no statement of how stress was determined; §2.2 p.5 and §2.3.2.3 contrast 'careful/slow speech' vs 'rapid speech' realisations of presyllables ('There is a transitional vowel of varying quality in the presyllable in careful speech ... but in rapid speech this transition disappears'), impressionistic, no instrumental measurement.
morph.stmt: Khmu is near-isolating with exclusively left-edge bound morphology: 'Affixes that are still productive... are a causative prefix, a descriptive prefix, and an instrumental infix. These affixes are considered to be derivational affixes. They do not indicate grammatical function but create new lexical items' (§3.1 p.25); all grammatical categories (aspect, modality, negation) are free preverbal particles and 'Even the presyllable itself tends to disappear and Khmu is now becoming a monosyllabic language' (p.25). No suffixes or enclitics of any kind are described.

tn.quote: In the Khmu dialect under study here I incline to say that it presents a case of register complex. Pitches alone cannot be used to characterise this aspect of Khmu phonology. ... Minimal pairs are found in words whose voice quality is that of 'breathy' versus 'clear' and whose pitch is that of 'lower' versus 'higher'. ... the Khmu registers can be classified into two contrastive types: tense register and lax register. Throughout this description tense register words will be marked by ´ and lax register words by `.
tn.cite: Suwilai Premsrirat. 1987. A Khmu Grammar. Papers in South-East Asian Linguistics No. 10: Khmu, a minority language of Thailand, pp. 1-143. Pacific Linguistics A-75. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-A75.1
tn.note: Analysed as a two-way register complex, not a fully developed tone system: tense (clear voice, high pitch) vs lax (breathy, mid/low pitch), minimal pairs on main syllables; word stress is final.

evidence_works.detail: A phonology sketch inside a syntax thesis. States that a phonological syllable is 'either monosyllabic which consists of one usually stressed main syllable or major syllable or bisyllable (which consists of a preliminary unstressed presyllable or minor syllable and a (following) stressed main syllable' (p.30) and that bisyllabic words consist of a presyllable/minor syllable 'and a (following) stressed main syllable or major syllable' (p.31): stress on the final main syllable, presyllable unstressed, i.e. the entry's 01 pattern. Says nothing about trisyllables or about any secondary stress. This Nan dialect is described with 'consonants, vowels and tones' (p.16) and 'There are 2 tones in this Khmu dialect because they are used to contrast individual lexical items or words (see minimal pairs)' (p.22), so it is a tone-contrast variety like the catalogued one.

evidence_works.work: Ong-Arj 1988, A phonology of Khmu Lue at Nan province (MA thesis, Mahidol University: pp. 21-23, 26-27, 39-40, 95, 100-101)
evidence_works.detail: Impressionistic field phonology. Placement: 'The stress in this language is treated as predictable. It occurs on every monosyllabic word. In two syllable words, it occurs on the last syllable' (p.100); 'Each stress group has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group' (p.101); the nuclear (major) syllable 'always occupies the final position in the stress group' (p.39); 'I have found only one trisyllabic word in Khmu Lue. Its structure is UUS' (p.40), i.e. 001. Refinement: a three-degree grading. 'The stress group in Khmu Lue may have from one to two syllables. It has only one stressed syllable as nucleus, and may have one preceding unstressed or weakly stressed as periphery' (p.21); 'Weakly stressed syllable is called minor syllable and the unstressed one is called presyllable' (p.22); 'The major syllable takes strong stress while the minor syllable takes weak stress and presyllable unstress' (p.40). The 'weak stress' is a property of the minor-syllable class, defined as 'a syllable which always takes weak stress. It can be either closed or open syllable' with four subtypes up to CV(:)(V)(C) (§4.3.2 p.26), as against the presyllable, 'a syllable which takes unstress' that precedes the major syllable and whose vowel is restricted to five qualities (§4.3.3 p.27); it sits inside a stress group that the author says has one stressed nucleus, so it is a periphery degree rather than a second stress. Suprasegmentals: this dialect has 'two phonemic registers: High clear and Low breathy' (p.95) and only intonational pitch contours (rising for yes-no questions, falling for statements, p.101), not lexical tone.
